# The Physics of Impact: When to Replace Bent Rims

Hitting a curb at low speed, even under 15 mph, creates a specific failure mode that differs significantly from high-speed impacts. The geometry of the damage suggests a localized deformation rather than a systemic shock event. In your case, the passenger-side front wheel shows a noticeable bend, while the rear counterpart on the same side is less affected. This asymmetry provides critical clues about the mechanics of the impact and informs the replacement strategy.

The primary question is whether to replace one or both rims. From an engineering standpoint, if the rim profile is visibly deformed enough to cause tire pressure loss, the structural integrity of that specific wheel is compromised. Aluminum wheels, in particular, are susceptible to "heat treating" issues where bending alters their temper, making them more brittle over time. If the front passenger rim was bent significantly enough to drop tire pressure from 32 PSI to roughly 29-30 PSI within 24 hours, air is escaping through micro-fractures created by the bend or a compromised bead seat.

Replacing only the front wheel is technically feasible, but it introduces handling dynamics issues. Your vehicle now has mismatched rolling radii. While modern ABS/ESP systems can compensate for minor differences in wheel size, a visibly bent rim often implies an out-of-round condition. An out-of-round wheel will cause pulsation in the brake pedal and steering wheel vibration, which are direct symptoms of uneven tire deformation against the road surface. If you replace only the front wheel, you must ensure the new wheel is perfectly round and true to avoid introducing a new fault into the system. However, replacing both wheels on the affected side (front and rear passenger) is often the safer long-term decision. This restores balance to the suspension geometry on that axle, ensuring that the impact force was not merely an outlier but part of a cascade of stress points.

Regarding the tires themselves, the situation requires a rigorous inspection before mounting them on new rims. A drop in pressure from 32 PSI to 29-30 PSI indicates a breach in the air-tight seal. This could be caused by the rim bending away from the tire bead or damage to the rubber sidewall where it contacted the curb. Even if the tire appears uninflated after being re-seated, you must verify that the tread depth and sidewall integrity are not compromised. A visual inspection for cracks in the white lettering area (if applicable) or bulges is mandatory. If the tire has suffered a "curb cut" where the rubber was sliced off the side wall, replacing the rim will not fix the failure; the tire must be replaced as well.

There is a trade-off here between cost and safety margins. Replacing just one wheel minimizes immediate expenditure but risks recurring pressure loss if the new wheel isn't perfectly matched or if the old tire was already damaged. Replacing both wheels ensures that the vehicle returns to its original dynamic specifications, eliminating variables related to weight distribution on that specific axle.

Before making a final decision, take the car to a shop that can measure the runout of the existing rim. If the lateral and radial runout exceeds industry standards (typically 0.7mm), the rim is out of tolerance regardless of appearance. In such cases, replacement is not optional; it is a safety requirement. If the old tire has any sign of sidewall damage, do not mount it on a new rim. The combination of a fresh wheel and a compromised tire can lead to sudden failure at highway speeds.

If you decide to proceed with repairs or replacements, ensure that the new wheels are balanced correctly. An unbalanced wheel transfers vibration through the hub bearings, which can accelerate wear on suspension components like tie rods and ball joints. Always verify that the new rims match the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) specifications for offset and backspacing to maintain proper steering geometry.

Ultimately, the visible bend in the front passenger wheel combined with the pressure drop suggests that the rim has lost its structural rigidity. The safest engineering approach is to replace the damaged front wheel and inspect the rear one closely. If the rear wheel shows even minor signs of runout or if the tire sidewall was impacted during the curb strike, replacing both wheels on the passenger side restores the vehicle's original safety envelope.
